newsitem.title: UK: Weak U.S. gasoline and flighty funds depress oil.
newsitem.headline: Weak U.S. gasoline and flighty funds depress oil.

text.p: Oil prices reversed early gains to end nearly $1 a barrel weaker on Wednesday as U.S. gasoline prices slid and investment funds looked for better returns in other markets.
January futures for benchmark North Sea Brent crude in London hit a high of $23.70 a barrel on Wednesday but then slumped in late trade to close at $22.50, down 84 cents on Tuesday's close.

Brokers said U.S. gasoline led the retreat as evidence of rising supply more than cancelled out the impact of a bullish combination of falling heating oil stocks and cold weather across the United States which prompted the early rally.
"U.S. gasoline went first as the market attempted to break through recent highs and failed," said a broker.
Although U.S. gasoline stocks also fell last week, industry data showed production rose to 7.78 million gallons a day from 7.43 million the previous week.
Strong equity and bond markets in the U.S. were also encouraging hedge fund managers to reduce their exposure to oil prices, brokers said.
"Equities and bonds are looking better because inflation prospects are better so some of the hedge funds may have decided they no longer need to hold raw materials," said one.

However, some traders said the continued cold blast, which brought early snow to parts of England on Tuesday, and news on Wednesday of another weekly fall in U.S. oil stocks, would continue to provide support to prices.
Oil prices have been hovering around their highest levels in more than six years as traders rush to replenish stocks which have fallen to their lowest levels in years.
The American Petroleum Institute (API) on Tuesday night said U.S. crude stocks fell 3.5 million barrels last week and stand 9.9 million below 1995 levels.

But more alarmingly, inventories of U.S. distillates, mostly heating oil, stand some 15 million barrels below last year. Traders worry that a repeat of last winter's frigid temperatures will leave the market short of heating fuel.
The high oil price -- which has stunned most analysts who had been expecting much lower prices -- has taken its toll on import costs of major consumers.
On Wednesday, U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said rising oil imports were mainly behind an increase in the U.S. trade gap in September.
He said since oil prices continued to climb in October, so the trade gap was sure to widen again.

"Oil prices have been going up and they have gone up again in October," Kantor said. "Therefore even based on the same volumes, we would have a larger deficit in oil in the month of October. It has a rather profound effect on our trade situation."

The price of imported crude to the U.S. rose to an average of $20.02 a barrel in September from $18.65 in August, while import volumes rose to eight million barrels per day from 7.4 million in August.
